style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive text) + amplified study form; bare-transliteration in amp with Strong's carried in notes (matching the ch.1 pilot); em-dashes used sparingly.
chapterNote: Chapter 26 is a gallery of three portraits drawn in vivid, almost cartoonish strokes. First the fool (vv. 1-12): honor sits on him as absurdly as snow in summer, and the famous paradox of vv. 4-5 -- answer him, do not answer him -- teaches that folly must be handled with discernment, not formula. Then the sluggard (vv. 13-16), who sees lions in the street and cannot lift his hand from the dish, yet thinks himself wiser than seven sages. Finally the troublemaker (vv. 17-28): the meddler, the deceiver who hides behind 'I was only joking,' and above all the whisperer whose gossip is fuel to a fire and whose smooth lips conceal a heart of seven abominations. The chapter ends with the proverb's iron justice: the pit-digger falls into his own pit, and the lying tongue destroys those it pretends to love.

1.text: Like snow in the heat of summer or rain at harvest time, so honor is altogether unfitting for a fool.
1.amp: Like snow in summer [qayits -- the dry hot season, the very time snow has no business falling] and like rain at harvest [qatsir -- the reaping season, when rain ruins the crop], so honor [kavod -- weight, glory, the esteem that gives a man standing] is not fitting [naveh -- comely, suitable] for a fool [kesil -- the thick-headed, morally dull man].
1.notes: kavod (H3519) literally means 'weight' -- honor is the social heft a man carries; to load it onto a kesil (H3684) is as out of season as summer snow (qayits, H7019) or harvest rain (qatsir, H7105), each a thing that arrives at exactly the wrong moment and does only harm.

2.text: Like a sparrow in restless flitting or a swallow in its darting, so an undeserved curse never lands.
2.amp: Like the sparrow [tsippor] in its fluttering [nud -- to wander, flit, never settling] and the swallow [deror] in its flying [uph -- to soar, dart through the air], so a curse [qelalah] without cause [chinnam -- groundless, gratuitous] shall not come to rest [bo -- come in, alight].
2.notes: chinnam (H2600) means 'for nothing, without cause' -- the same word for the gang's gratuitous violence in 1:11. A curse hurled without just ground has no place to land (bo, H935); like a flitting bird (nud, H5110) it never comes home to roost. God's moral order will not let groundless cursing stick.

3.text: What the whip is to the horse and the bridle to the donkey, the rod is to the back of fools.
3.amp: A whip for the horse [sus], a bridle [meteg -- the bit that turns the head] for the donkey [chamor], and a rod [shevet -- the disciplining staff] for the back [gev] of fools [kesil].
3.notes: shevet (H7626) is the shepherd's rod and the ruler's scepter -- the same word later imaged for correction. The proverb is deliberately blunt: as surely as a horse needs the whip and a donkey the bit, the kesil (H3684) is reached only through the rod, because reasoning has failed to move him.

4.text: Do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you yourself will become just like him.
4.amp: Do not answer [anah -- respond, reply] a fool [kesil] according to his folly [ivvelet -- his moral foolishness], lest you also become like [shavah -- be made equal, leveled] to him.
4.notes: the first half of the famous paradox (vv. 4-5). To answer a fool on his own terms -- stooping to his logic and his heat -- is to be dragged down to his level (shavah, H7737, to be made equal). ivvelet (H200) is not mere ignorance but a stubborn moral folly that infects whoever engages it carelessly.

5.text: Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he become wise in his own eyes.
5.amp: Answer [anah] a fool [kesil] according to his folly [ivvelet], lest he be wise [chakam] in his own eyes [ayin -- the eye, here the seat of self-estimate].
5.notes: the second half of the paradox, set side by side with v. 4 on purpose: the two are not a contradiction but a pair of cases requiring discernment. Sometimes folly must be left unanswered (v. 4); sometimes it must be met head-on, lest silence let the fool think himself wise (chakam, H2450) in his own ayin (H5869). Wisdom is knowing which moment is which.

6.text: Whoever sends a message by the hand of a fool cuts off his own feet and drinks down violence.
6.amp: He that sends [shalach -- dispatch, send off] a message [davar -- word, matter, errand] by the hand of a fool [kesil] cuts off [qatsah] the feet [regel] and drinks down [shatah] violence [chamas -- ruinous wrong, harm done].
6.notes: chamas (H2555) is violent injustice -- the very word that filled the earth before the Flood (Gen 6:11). To trust a kesil (H3684) with your errand is self-mutilation: you lose your own footing (regel, H7272) and swallow the damage as if drinking it down (shatah, H8354), because the fool will mangle whatever he carries.

7.text: Like the legs of a lame man that dangle useless, so is a proverb in the mouth of fools.
7.amp: The legs [shoq -- the thighs, the limbs meant for walking] of the lame [pisseach] hang limp and unequal [dalah -- hang down, dangle slack]: so is a proverb [mashal] in the mouth [peh] of fools [kesil].
7.notes: a mashal (H4912) is a wisdom-saying meant to carry a man forward, just as legs are meant to walk; but in a fool's peh (H6310) it dangles uselessly, like the limp limbs (shoq, H7785) of the lame -- present, but powerless to move him anywhere good. The truth is sound; the bearer cannot carry it.

8.text: Like binding a stone fast in a sling, so is the giving of honor to a fool.
8.amp: As one who binds [tsarar -- bind tight, fasten] a stone [even] in a sling [margemah -- the heap or sling of stones], so is he who gives [natan] honor [kavod] to a fool [kesil].
8.notes: a stone is meant to fly from the sling, not be lashed into it -- tie it fast (tsarar, H6887) and the weapon is worse than useless, even dangerous to the slinger. So honor (kavod, H3519) bound onto a kesil (H3684) defeats its whole purpose and recoils on the one who bestowed it; cf. v. 1, the chapter's other 'honor for a fool' proverb.

9.text: Like a thornbush brandished in the hand of a drunkard, so is a proverb in the mouth of fools.
9.amp: As a thorn [choach -- a bramble, a thornbush] comes up [alah -- rises, is lifted] into the hand of a drunkard [shikkor], so is a proverb [mashal] in the mouth [peh] of fools [kesil].
9.notes: paired with v. 7, this is the second proverb on a mashal (H4912) in a fool's peh (H6310). A drunk man waving a thornbush wounds himself and everyone near him -- he cannot handle even what is in his own hand. So a fool wielding a wise saying does harm with it, slashing where it should heal.

10.text: Like an archer who wounds everyone at random, so is he who hires a fool or hires any passerby.
10.amp: Like a great archer [rav -- great, or the master who shoots] who pierces all [chul -- writhe, wound, whirl down], so is he who hires [sakar] the fool [kesil] and hires the transgressors [avar -- those who pass by, the wandering hireling].
10.notes: a famously difficult verse; rendered with the WEB's archer image. The point of the consonants is that hiring a kesil (H3684) or a random passerby (avar, H5674) is as reckless as loosing arrows into a crowd -- you wound indiscriminately, yourself included, because you have handed responsibility to one who cannot bear it.

11.text: As a dog goes back to its own vomit, so a fool repeats his folly again and again.
11.amp: As a dog [kelev] returns [shuv -- turn back, go again] to its vomit [qe], so a fool [kesil] repeats [shanah -- does a second time, iterates] his folly [ivvelet].
11.notes: shuv (H7725) is the great turning-verb -- normally the word for repentance; here it is repentance's grim parody, a turning back not to God but to one's own filth. Peter cites this proverb of the false teacher who returns to corruption (2 Pet 2:22). The fool's tragedy is the loop: his ivvelet (H200) is not a stumble but a cycle he keeps choosing.

12.text: Have you ever met a man convinced of his own wisdom? Even a fool stands a better chance than he does.
12.amp: Do you see [raah -- look at, observe] a man [ish] wise [chakam] in his own eyes [ayin]? There is more hope [tiqvah -- expectation, a stretched-out cord of hope] for a fool [kesil] than for him.
12.notes: the climax of the fool-gallery (vv. 1-12), and its sharpest turn: worse than the kesil (H3684) is the man wise in his own ayin (H5869). The fool may yet be taught; the self-satisfied man has bolted the only door wisdom enters by. tiqvah (H8615) is hope as a cord stretched toward a future -- and even the fool's cord is longer than the conceited man's; cf. 3:7, 'be not wise in your own eyes.'

13.text: The sluggard says, 'There's a lion in the road! A lion is prowling the open streets!'
13.amp: The sluggard [atsel -- the lazy man, the sloth] says [amar], 'There is a lion [shachal -- a roaring lion] in the way [derek]; a lion [ari] is loose in the open squares [rechov]!'
13.notes: the chapter turns from fool to sluggard (vv. 13-16). The atsel (H6102) is a master of excuses: he conjures a lion (shachal, H7826) in the derek (H1870) to justify never leaving home. The peril is imaginary, but it serves perfectly -- any pretext will do for the man who has already decided not to work; cf. 22:13, where the lion excuse recurs.

14.text: As a door turns on its hinges, so the sluggard turns over on his bed.
14.amp: As the door [delet] turns [savav -- swing around, rotate, go in a circle] upon its hinges [tsir], so does the sluggard [atsel] upon his bed [mittah].
14.notes: savav (H5437) is to go round and round -- and that is the whole picture: the door swings, swings, and goes nowhere, fastened forever to the same frame. So the atsel (H6102) rolls on his mittah (H4296), busy with motion that carries him not one step forward. He is active, but only in place.

15.text: Having sunk his hand down into the bowl, the sluggard finds the journey back to his mouth too exhausting to finish.
15.amp: The sluggard [atsel] buries [taman -- hide, sink, conceal] his hand in the dish [tsallachat -- the bowl]; it wearies [laah -- to be exhausted, worn out] him to bring it back [shuv] to his mouth [peh].
15.notes: comic hyperbole sharpening v. 14: the atsel (H6102) has sunk (taman, H2934) his hand into the food, yet finds the few inches back to his peh (H6310) too exhausting (laah, H3811) to complete. Laziness is not merely unproductive; it grows until it defeats even self-interest, even eating.

16.text: The sluggard is wiser in his own eyes than seven men who answer with sound judgment.
16.amp: The sluggard [atsel] is wiser [chakam] in his own eyes [ayin] than seven [sheva -- seven, the number of fullness] men who can give back [shuv] a reason [taam -- discernment, good sense, sound judgment].
16.notes: the sluggard shares the fool's fatal disease of v. 12 -- wisdom in his own ayin (H5869). Seven (sheva, H7651) is the number of completeness: he ranks himself above a full council of discerning men. taam (H2940) is the faculty of good taste in judgment; the atsel (H6102) has none, yet is sure he has more than anyone.

17.text: Like grabbing a passing dog by the ears is the man who meddles in a quarrel that is none of his own.
17.amp: Like one who seizes [chazaq -- grip hard, take firm hold] a dog [kelev] by the ears [ozen] is he who passes by [avar] and meddles [avar -- crosses over, mixes himself in] in a strife [riv -- a dispute, a legal quarrel] not his own.
17.notes: the gossip-and-strife section opens (vv. 17-28). The pun is in the Hebrew: the meddler 'passes by' and 'crosses into' (both avar, H5674) a quarrel. To grab a stray dog by the ears (chazaq, H2388) is to guarantee a bite you brought entirely on yourself. A riv (H7379) not your own is exactly such a dog.

18.text: Like a madman flinging deadly firebrands, arrows, and death,
18.amp: Like a madman [lahah -- one raving, out of his senses] who flings [yarah -- throw, shoot] firebrands [zeq -- flaming darts, burning sparks], arrows [chets], and death [mavet],
18.notes: vv. 18-19 form a single picture. yarah (H3384) means both 'shoot' and 'teach' -- but here it is a deranged man (lahah, H3856) loosing lethal sparks (zeq, H2131) and arrows at random. The setup waits for v. 19 to name who this maniac actually is.

19.text: so is the man who deceives his neighbor and then says, 'I was only joking!'
19.amp: so is the man [ish] who deceives [ramah -- beguile, deal treacherously with] his neighbor [rea -- friend, fellow] and says [amar], 'Am I not just playing [sachaq -- laughing, jesting, making sport]?'
19.notes: the sting lands: the cheat who hides behind 'I was only joking' (sachaq, H7832) is no harmless jokester but the madman of v. 18, flinging real death at his rea (H7453). The plea of jest is itself part of the treachery (ramah, H7411) -- weaponizing humor to dodge the harm one meant to do.

20.text: For lack of wood the fire goes out, and where there is no whisperer, strife falls silent.
20.amp: Where there is no [ephes -- a ceasing, an end of] wood [ets] the fire [esh] goes out [kavah -- be quenched, die down]; and where there is no whisperer [nirgan -- gossip, slanderer, murmurer], strife [madon -- contention, discord] grows silent [shataq -- quiets, falls still].
20.notes: the central insight of the gossip section: contention is a fire (esh, H784), and the nirgan (H5372), the whisperer, is its fuel. Cut off the wood (ets, H6086) and the flame dies (kavah, H3518); remove the gossip and the quarrel (madon, H4066) simply goes quiet (shataq, H8367). Strife does not sustain itself -- someone keeps feeding it.

21.text: As charcoal is to embers and wood is to fire, so a quarrelsome man is for kindling strife.
21.amp: As coals [pecham -- charcoal] are to burning embers [gechalim], and wood [ets] to fire [esh], so is a contentious [midyan -- quarrelsome] man [ish] to kindle [charar -- set ablaze, inflame] strife [riv].
21.notes: the exact inverse of v. 20. If no whisperer means no fire, the contentious man (midyan, H4079) is the live coal (pecham, H6352) that sets it roaring. charar (H2787) is to scorch and inflame: such a man does not merely find conflict, he manufactures it, supplying the very fuel that keeps riv (H7379) burning.

22.text: The words of a whisperer are like dainty morsels; they slide down into the innermost chambers of the body.
22.amp: The words [davar] of a whisperer [nirgan -- gossip, slanderer] are like choice morsels [lacham -- swallowed greedily, dainty bits]; they go down [yarad -- descend, sink] into the inner chambers [cheder -- the innermost rooms] of the belly [beten -- the gut, the deepest self].
22.notes: a near-verbatim repeat of 18:8, underscoring the theme. Gossip is delicious -- we swallow the nirgan's (H5372) words like dainties -- and that is its danger: they sink (yarad, H3381) past the ears into the cheder (H2315), the locked inner rooms of the beten (H990), where they lodge and breed suspicion long after the telling.

23.text: Like a glaze of silver dross over a clay pot are fervent lips joined to an evil heart.
23.amp: Like silver dross [kesef sigim -- the worthless slag skimmed off silver] glazing [tsaphah -- overlay, coat] an earthen pot [cheres -- common pottery, a potsherd] are burning [dalaq -- fervent, fiery, ardent] lips [saphah] and an evil [ra] heart [lev].
23.notes: the ancients glazed cheap pottery (cheres, H2789) to mimic precious metal. So warm, glowing speech (dalaq, H1814, 'burning' lips) laid over a wicked lev (H3820) is only slag-glaze (sigim, H5509) on clay -- a thin, shining lie over something common and cracked. The charm is real; the worth is not.

24.text: The one who hates disguises himself with his lips, but inside he harbors deceit;
24.amp: He that hates [sane -- holds hostility, is an enemy] dissembles [nakar -- makes himself unrecognizable, masks himself] with his lips [saphah], and lays up [shith -- set, store, deposit] deceit [mirmah -- treachery, fraud] within him [qerev -- his inward parts];
24.notes: vv. 24-26 trace the hidden hater. nakar (H5234) can mean both 'recognize' and 'feign as foreign' -- here he makes his own face strange, masking hatred with friendly saphah (H8193) while storing (shith, H7896) treachery (mirmah, H4820) deep in his qerev (H7130). The lips perform; the gut plots.

25.text: When his voice turns gracious, do not believe him, for seven abominations fill his heart.
25.amp: When he makes his voice [qol] gracious [chanan -- charming, full of favor], do not believe [aman -- trust, rely on, hold firm] him; for seven [sheva -- the full number] abominations [toevah -- detestable things] are in his heart [lev].
25.notes: the warning of v. 24 made practical: when the hater's qol (H6963) turns sweet (chanan, H2603), refuse to entrust yourself (aman, H539) to it. Seven (sheva, H7651) toevot (H8441) -- a full complement of things the LORD detests (cf. 6:16-19) -- fill the lev (H3820) the charm is meant to hide. The smoother the voice, the deeper the danger.

26.text: Though his hatred is masked by deceit, his wickedness will be laid bare before the whole assembly.
26.amp: Though his hatred [sinah] is covered [kasah -- concealed, hidden] by deceit [mashshaon -- guile, treachery], his wickedness [ra] shall be uncovered [galah -- revealed, exposed, also: sent into exile] before the whole assembly [qahal -- the gathered congregation].
26.notes: kasah (H3680), to cover, meets its opposite galah (H1540), to uncover -- the same verb used for exile, a dragging out into the open. However well the hater hides his sinah (H8135), the day comes when his ra (H7451) is exposed before the qahal (H6951), the public assembly. Concealment has an expiration; truth surfaces.

27.text: Whoever digs a pit will fall into it, and the one who rolls a stone -- it rolls back upon him.
27.amp: Whoever digs [karah -- dig out, excavate] a pit [shachat -- a trap-pit, a snare] shall fall [naphal] into it; and he who rolls [galal -- roll along] a stone [even], it returns [shuv] upon him.
27.notes: the proverb's iron law of recoil: the trap-pit (shachat, H7845) dug for another (karah, H3738) swallows its own digger, and the stone heaved at someone (galal, H1556) rolls back (shuv, H7725) to crush the one who shoved it. Sin is a boomerang; cf. Ps 7:15-16; 57:6. The schemer is undone by his own scheme.

28.text: A lying tongue hates the very ones it crushes, and a flattering mouth brings on ruin.
28.amp: A lying [sheqer -- false, deceitful] tongue [lashon] hates [sane] those it crushes [daka -- the bruised, the broken ones it afflicts]; and a flattering [chalaq -- smooth, slippery] mouth [peh] works [asah -- makes, brings about] ruin [midcheh -- overthrow, downfall].
28.notes: the chapter closes by exposing two faces of the deceitful tongue (lashon, H3956). The liar secretly hates (sane, H8130) the very people his sheqer (H8267) wounds; and the smooth, flattering peh (H6310) -- chalaq (H2509), 'slippery' -- is no kindness but a maker (asah, H6213) of ruin (midcheh, H4072). Harsh truth heals; smooth falsehood destroys.
